en-t9.subject: English A: Literature
en-t9.question: Write one analytical paragraph: how does Carroll use direct speech and invented words to present the son's quest as both heroic and comic? Quote exactly from the poem, including its spoken lines. Write no more than 300 words.

supplied_texts.title: Jabberwocky (poem, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Lewis Carroll
supplied_texts.text:
'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

"Beware the Jabberwock, my son!
The jaws that bite, the claws that catch!
Beware the Jubjub bird, and shun
The frumious Bandersnatch!"

He took his vorpal sword in hand:
Long time the manxome foe he sought—
So rested he by the Tumtum tree,
And stood awhile in thought.

And, as in uffish thought he stood,
The Jabberwock, with eyes of flame,
Came whiffling through the tulgey wood,
And burbled as it came!

One, two! One, two! And through and through
The vorpal blade went snicker-snack!
He left it dead, and with its head
He went galumphing back.

"And hast thou slain the Jabberwock?
Come to my arms, my beamish boy!
O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"
He chortled in his joy.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

en-t9.response_text: Carroll presents the son's quest as a heroic rite whose solemnity is continually undercut by its own language, so that it reads as both grave duty and comic performance. The speaker's warning establishes the seriousness: "Beware the Jabberwock, my son!" The imperative and the direct address place the quest within a line of inherited instruction. The warning then makes the threat physical through ordinary words, "The jaws that bite, the claws that catch!", whose plain verbs of biting and catching imagine a real body. Yet the other enemies arrive as invented names, "the Jubjub bird" and "The frumious Bandersnatch!", which have no dictionary meaning. The adjective "frumious" sounds fierce while telling the listener nothing he can use, so the solemnity is attached to words that cannot be understood. This suggests that the authority of the warning outruns its content, and the reader is encouraged to see the danger as real and the instruction as empty. The speaker's welcome sustains the pattern. "And hast thou slain the Jabberwock?" adopts the archaic "hast thou" of heroic romance, and "my beamish boy" with "O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!" sounds like a grand celebration. Yet "beamish" and "frabjous" are invented adjectives, and "Callooh! Callay!" refers to nothing, so the acclaim is ceremony without content. Carroll then reports the response, "He chortled in his joy", where a verb of gleeful laughter replaces the expected verb of triumph. Direct speech thus supplies the heroic form, a warning and a welcome, while invented words drain that form of content, so that admiration and laughter remain held together.

en-t10.subject: English A: Literature
en-t10.question: Write one analytical paragraph on how Marvell uses hyperbole, and the turn at 'But at my back', to build the speaker's argument about time. Use quotations from the extract. Keep to about 250 words.

supplied_texts.title: To His Coy Mistress, lines 1-32 (extract, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Andrew Marvell
supplied_texts.text:
Had we but world enough and time,
This coyness, lady, were no crime.
We would sit down, and think which way
To walk, and pass our long love's day.
Thou by the Indian Ganges' side
Shouldst rubies find; I by the tide
Of Humber would complain. I would
Love you ten years before the flood,
And you should, if you please, refuse
Till the conversion of the Jews.
My vegetable love should grow
Vaster than empires and more slow;
An hundred years should go to praise
Thine eyes, and on thy forehead gaze;
Two hundred to adore each breast,
But thirty thousand to the rest;
An age at least to every part,
And the last age should show your heart.
For, lady, you deserve this state,
Nor would I love at lower rate.

But at my back I always hear
Time's wingèd chariot hurrying near;
And yonder all before us lie
Deserts of vast eternity.
Thy beauty shall no more be found;
Nor, in thy marble vault, shall sound
My echoing song; then worms shall try
That long-preserved virginity,
And your quaint honour turn to dust,
And into ashes all my lust;
The grave's a fine and private place,
But none, I think, do there embrace.

en-t10.response_text: Marvell builds the speaker's argument about time on hyperbole, then reverses it at the turn, so that the time he has invented becomes the reason to act now. The courtship's extravagance sets up a premise of limitless time: "An hundred years should go to praise / Thine eyes, and on thy forehead gaze;" and "Two hundred to adore each breast, / But thirty thousand to the rest". The numbers measure love in years, and "praise" and "adore", which conventionally carry devotional meaning, become units of a time budget. The key word is "rest", a vague catch-all that absorbs the whole body into a sum so large that it is plainly absurd. Because the exaggeration is evidently impossible, the reader is encouraged to see the premise as a fantasy in which the lady's coyness "were no crime". The turn then arrives with the conjunction "But", which exposes that premise. The phrase "at my back" is spatially precise: time lies behind the speaker, sensed through hearing ("I always hear") rather than seen, and "wingèd" conventionally suggests speed, so time changes from something that can be stretched into a pursuer that cannot be outrun. The next line makes the future equally hostile: "Deserts of vast eternity." The desert is conventionally barren, and "vast" repeats the scale of the hyperbole as a void rather than an abundance. The same magnitude that made love seem limitless now makes time's loss inescapable, so the argument moves from persuasion to urgency.

en-p4.subject: English A: Literature
en-p4.question: A History student is studying the Second Boer War (1899-1902) and the men who volunteered to fight in it. In one analytical paragraph of no more than 250 words, show how Hardy's 'The Man He Killed' (1902) uses a colloquial dramatic monologue to present the speaker's reasons for enlisting and his view of the man he shot. Quote exactly from the poem. The paragraph will be passed to the History specialist as context.

supplied_texts.title: The Man He Killed (poem, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Thomas Hardy
supplied_texts.text:
"Had he and I but met
By some old ancient inn,
We should have sat us down to wet
Right many a nipperkin!

"But ranged as infantry,
And staring face to face,
I shot at him as he at me,
And killed him in his place.

"I shot him dead because—
Because he was my foe,
Just so: my foe of course he was;
That's clear enough; although

"He thought he'd 'list, perhaps,
Off-hand like—just as I—
Was out of work—had sold his traps—
No other reason why.

"Yes; quaint and curious war is!
You shoot a fellow down
You'd treat if met where any bar is,
Or help to half-a-crown."

en-p4.response_text: Hardy's dramatic monologue lets the speaker justify the killing in casual terms, and the casualness exposes a motive of poverty and a view of the enemy that his justification cannot sustain. The motive is presented through a colloquial parallel: "He thought he'd 'list, perhaps, / Off-hand like—just as I— / Was out of work—had sold his traps—". The clipped "'list" makes enlisting sound impulsive, while "just as I" implies that the speaker's own reason matches the enemy's. The key word "traps", which conventionally denotes snares but in colloquial use means a man's gear and belongings, suggests a man who has sold his belongings for want of work, so poverty becomes the motive, as the closing "No other reason why" confirms. The view of the enemy is built through the repetition of "foe": "I shot him dead because— / Because he was my foe, / Just so: my foe of course he was". Foe should supply a reason for killing, but it only restates the killing, so the justification becomes circular, and the unfinished "although" that ends the stanza shows a speaker who does not complete his argument. The opening conditional, "Had he and I but met", imagines the man as a drinking companion, which suggests the speaker sees the enemy as a man like himself. The final stanza sets the killing beside a social courtesy, "You shoot a fellow down / You'd treat if met where any bar is", so the colloquial voice comfortably holds a contradiction.

hi-t9.subject: History
hi-t9.question: To what extent did Stalin's Five-Year Plans transform Soviet heavy industry between 1928 and 1941? Write one body paragraph only, following your method, in no more than 350 words, with dated and quantified evidence.
hi-t9.response_text: The Five-Year Plans transformed Soviet heavy industry to a large extent in scale and geography, but far less in efficiency and in the quality of its output. Between 1928 and 1932 official figures show pig iron rising from about 3.3 million tonnes to about 6.2 million, steel from about 4.3 million to 5.9 million and coal from about 35 million tonnes to about 64 million. These totals fell short of the First Plan's original target of about 10 million tonnes of pig iron, and later Western reassessments reduced the growth that the official series claimed, yet the expansion was real and it was directed by state investment rather than by market demand. The geography changed as well. Magnitogorsk, built on an iron-ore mountain in the southern Urals, lit its first blast furnace in 1932, and the Second Five-Year Plan of 1933 to 1937 pushed coal output to about 128 million tonnes by 1937. The eastward shift meant that the Urals and the Kuznetsk basin could take on production when the German invasion of 22 June 1941 overran the Donbas and Ukrainian works. Against this, the growth was extensive rather than intensive: it relied on migrant peasant labour, on forced labour from the camps and on imported machinery and foreign engineers, and output per worker rose far more slowly than the tonnages on most estimates. Judged by the criterion of military and industrial capacity by 1941, the plans achieved a great deal; judged by efficiency, they achieved much less. The transformation was therefore largely quantitative and spatial, and it created a heavy-industrial base without yet making that base efficient. Dates and figures are from memory; verify them against your notes before use.

hi-t10.subject: History
hi-t10.question: Outline, with dated and quantified evidence, the growth of the railway network in Britain between 1830 and 1870. Write no more than 200 words and give a judgement on which decade saw the most decisive expansion.
hi-t10.response_text: Railway growth in Britain between 1830 and 1870 came in phases, and the 1840s gave the network its shape. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in September 1830 over 31 miles, the first inter-city line worked by steam locomotives on a timetable. The network then grew from almost nothing: the London and Birmingham Railway opened in 1838, and the Great Western reached Bristol in 1841. Route mileage was about 1,500 by 1840 and about 6,000 by 1850 (from memory; check your notes). The 1840s, which included the Railway Mania of 1845 to 1847, added roughly 4,500 miles, more than any other decade of the period, and by 1848 a line ran from London through Carlisle to Glasgow. The 1850s and 1860s took the network to about 13,000 miles by 1870, but largely through branches and extensions to an existing framework. The 1840s were the most decisive decade. Measured by what the network could do, carrying traffic between the main cities, they created the trunk routes that later growth filled in, whereas the 1830s, though faster in relative terms, built only the first links.

hi-p4.subject: History
hi-p4.question: You have received the English specialist's analytical paragraph on Hardy's 'The Man He Killed' (1902) through the hub; it is supplied to you as the document peer:en-p4. In one paragraph of no more than 220 words, outline for a literature student the historical context of what the English specialist identifies (the Second Boer War of 1899 to 1902, voluntary enlistment and unemployment among working-class recruits, and the scale of British losses), with dated evidence labelled from memory as your method requires. Where you draw on the English specialist's paragraph, quote it exactly and attribute it to the English specialist.
hi-p4.response_text: The English specialist's paragraph identifies the speaker's motive as poverty: the casualness "exposes a motive of poverty", and the key word "traps" suggests a man who "sold his belongings for want of work". The historical setting is my own addition, not part of that paragraph. The Second Boer War ran from 11 October 1899 to the Peace of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902 (from memory; check your notes), so the poem's 1902 date falls at the war's close. Reverses in December 1899, including the Highland Brigade's defeat at Magersfontein on 11 December (from memory), helped drive the call for volunteers, and the Imperial Yeomanry's first contingents sailed in early 1900 (from memory). A regular private's pay of about a shilling a day (from memory) was a real draw for men without work, though historians dispute how far unemployment, rather than patriotism or adventure, drove enlistment. The losses were heavy: roughly 22,000 British and imperial deaths, the large majority from disease, chiefly enteric fever (from memory; approximate, and sources differ). Against that toll, Hardy's speaker calls the conflict a "quaint and curious war", a line that reads as a sardonic frame for a war that killed far more men through disease than in battle.
